children: Money is back on the Federal Reserve’s dashboard but is unlikely to drive monetary policy unless growth in monetary aggregates accelerates sharply or collapses, according to Pantheon Macroeconomics.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said last month that “money matters,” arguing policymakers should pay greater attention to money created by the central bank and financial system.

That echoed arguments by former Fed Governor Stephen Miran and co-authors Peter Ireland and Nouriel Roubini that monetary aggregates can still provide useful information on growth and inflation. Pantheon economists Samuel Tombs and Oliver Allen said money growth had now normalized after the pandemic-era surge.

M2 money growth was running at just over 5% year over year, slightly below its pre-pandemic average of just over 6%, while M4 Divisia growth was around 7.5%, above its pre-pandemic average of about 5%, according to Pantheon. The report said M2, or its Divisia alternative, remained the most informative single measure for assessing potential implications for activity and inflation.

Pantheon said current money growth provided “little reason to worry about economic overheating” and that persistent inflation was difficult to attribute to excessively rapid money growth. The economists also said there was no remaining overhang of “excess money” from the pandemic, with most measures of money velocity having returned to pre-pandemic levels.

As a result, Pantheon said money was likely to earn a place among indicators the Federal Open Market Committee watches closely, but was “unlikely to steer the ship” given the lack of a strong signal in either direction.

The economists continued to expect the Fed to ease monetary policy next year after a possible further tightening this year. They said any such pivot would be driven by more encouraging inflation data and weakening labor-market conditions rather than monetary indicators.

title: Money returns to Fed dashboard but won't steer policy, Pantheon says
